facts.statement: The fossil remains of Plesiolophus were discovered by Wendy Sloboda near Warner, Alberta, Canada.
facts.quote: The Plesiolophus fossil material was discovered by Wendy Sloboda in the outcrops of the Oldman Formation, part of the Belly River Group, near Warner, Alberta, Canada.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen is housed at the Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology under the accession number TMP 2016.023.0039.
facts.quote: The specimen is housed in the Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology, where it is permanently accessioned as specimen TMP 2016.023.0039.

facts.statement: The genus Plesiolophus contains only one species, P. warnerensis, which is known from a partial skull.
facts.quote: The genus contains a single species, Plesiolophus warnerensis, known from a partial skull.

facts.statement: The fossil material represents the first diagnostic remains of an adult lambeosaurine from the Oldman Formation.
Plesiolophus lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the Campanian age.
Plesiolophus lived between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Campanian (83.6 to 72.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: Plesiolophus fossils come from the Oldman Formation, which lies beneath the Dinosaur Park Formation.
The parent group of Plesiolophus is the tribe Parasaurolophini.
Plesiolophus belongs to the family Hadrosauridae.
Plesiolophus is classified within the class Ornithischia.
Phylogenetic analysis places Plesiolophus as the basalmost member of an exclusively North American clade within Parasaurolophini.
facts.quote: Their strict consensus tree, which obtained better-resolved results, recovered the Asian Charonosaurus as the earliest-diverging member of the lambeosaurine clade Parasaurolophini. It is followed by an exclusively North American clade, of which Plesiolophus is the basalmost member.
